lead: Low-temperature combustion (LTC) is a way to burn fuel that avoids NOx and soot at the same time. It premixes and dilutes the charge so that no part of it is rich enough to make soot or hot enough to make NOx. The price is control: ignition is set by the chemistry of the charge, not by a spark or an injection pulse. HCCI and RCCI are the two forms named in exam syllabi; PCCI lies between them and the ordinary diesel.
prereq: You need: the soot and NOx routes (formation of CO, HC and NOx, smoke and particulate matter) and the dual-fuel idea (dual fuel and multi-fuel engines).

sections.h3: The φ–T map and the soot–NOx trade-off

blocks.text: Think of every small parcel of gas in the cylinder as a point on a map of local equivalence ratio φ against local temperature T. Soot forms in an island of rich, hot states, roughly φ above 2 at 1600 to 2600 K. NO forms in a band of hot states with oxygen to spare, roughly above 2200 K at φ near or below 1. Both regions are about local gas, not the average of the cylinder.

A conventional diesel spray crosses both. Its core passes through the soot island; its flame sheet, burning near stoichiometric, passes through the NOx band. Cooling the charge with EGR moves the flame out of the NOx band but leaves the core rich, so soot survives; adding air or retarding does the opposite. This is the soot–NOx trade-off. To beat it, the charge must be both lean (or well mixed, so no parcel is rich) and cool (peak below about 2000 K, held there by dilution). That region is the LTC window.

Efficiency can still be diesel-like: the engine runs unthrottled at a high compression ratio, and the lean, cool gas loses less heat. The difficulty is ignition, because a lean, cool mixture ignites slowly and its timing drifts with temperature.

HCCI mixes fuel and air before compression, like a petrol engine, and ignites it by compression heat, like a diesel. The charge is lean, φ about 0.2 to 0.5, or diluted with EGR. There is no spark and no flame front: the whole charge reaches self-ignition almost together and burns in a few crank degrees. Its timing follows the chemistry:

blocks.where: τ is the ignition delay; A a constant for the fuel and pressure; E/R the activation temperature, about 15 000 K here; T the charge temperature in K. A small rise in T shortens τ sharply.

blocks.text: The control levers are all indirect: intake air temperature, the EGR rate, hot residual gas trapped by variable valve timing, the compression ratio and the fuel’s reactivity. None acts on a single cycle like a spark does.

items: Gains: near-zero NOx and soot; diesel-like efficiency; low pumping loss.

Costs: high HC and CO at light load, because the coolest parts of the charge, near the walls and in crevices, never finish burning; violent pressure rise (ringing) at high load; a narrow load range; hard cold starts.

blocks.text: No production car runs pure HCCI. The nearest is spark-controlled compression ignition (Mazda’s SPCCI petrol engine, sold since 2019), where a small spark-lit flame compresses the rest of a lean charge into self-ignition at the chosen moment.

PCCI (premixed charge compression ignition) uses one fuel injected early, so it has time to mix before it ignites. The charge is partly premixed: soot is lower than in a normal diesel because the rich core is smaller, but some φ gradient remains, and ignition is still set by chemistry.

RCCI (reactivity controlled compression ignition) uses two fuels of different reactivity. A low-reactivity fuel (petrol, ethanol or natural gas) is port-injected to make a lean premixed charge. A high-reactivity fuel (diesel) is injected directly, once or twice, early enough to mix partly. Ignition starts where the diesel share is highest and spreads through the gradient of reactivity, which spreads out the heat release. Changing the ratio of the two fuels from cycle to cycle, and the diesel timing, sets the burn: more port fuel makes the charge less reactive and later. This gives RCCI a wider load range than HCCI and a real control lever. RCCI is still a research and demonstration strategy, not yet in production.

RCCI looks like the dual-fuel engine but works differently: there the diesel pilot lights a flame that travels through the gas; in RCCI the whole charge self-ignites in sequence, from more to less reactive parcels, with no flame front. A useful single number is the global reactivity, the primary reference fuel (PRF) number of the blend in the cylinder; with iso-octane (PRF 100) and n-heptane (PRF 0) it equals the iso-octane mass share × 100.

examples.question: Two HCCI runs have the same charge pressure. Run 1 has a charge temperature of 900 K, run 2 of 950 K. The ignition delay follows τ = A exp(E/RT) with E/R = 15 000 K. Find τ<sub>900</sub> ÷ τ<sub>950</sub> and say what it means for control.
steps: Ratio: τ<sub>900</sub> ÷ τ<sub>950</sub> = exp[(E/R)(1/900 − 1/950)], because A cancels.
A 50 K warmer charge ignites 2.4 times sooner, so a few kelvin of intake drift move the burn by crank degrees.
examples.answer: τ<sub>900</sub> ÷ τ<sub>950</sub> ≈ 2.4: HCCI needs intake temperature held within a few kelvin.

examples.question: A research RCCI engine gets 24 mg of iso-octane (PRF 100) per cycle through the port and 6 mg of n-heptane (PRF 0) by direct injection. Find the premixed ratio and the global PRF. At higher load the controller moves to 27 mg and 3 mg: what happens to the global reactivity and the burn?
steps: Premixed ratio = port fuel ÷ total fuel = 24 ÷ (24 + 6) = 0.80.

A higher PRF means a less reactive charge: ignition comes later and the heat release is slower, which keeps the pressure rise rate down at the higher load. (The two fuels have nearly equal LHV, about 44 MJ/kg, so the total energy is unchanged.)
examples.answer: The premixed ratio is 0.80 and the global PRF 80; moving to PRF 90 at high load retards and slows the burn, which is how RCCI avoids the ringing that limits HCCI.

traps: Calling HCCI a lean spark-ignition engine: there is no spark and no flame front; the charge self-ignites.
Saying cooling alone removes soot: a rich parcel still makes soot; LTC needs a lean, well-mixed charge as well as a low temperature.
Saying LTC makes NOx exactly zero: it keeps the peak below the fast NO range, so NOx is very low, not zero.
Calling ringing ordinary knock: it is a very fast pressure rise from the whole charge burning at once.
Describing RCCI as a pilot lighting a gas: its two fuels are chosen for their reactivity gradient, and the ratio is changed with load.

quiz.q: What does HCCI stand for, and what ignites the charge?
quiz.a: Homogeneous charge compression ignition; the heat of compression brings the whole lean charge to self-ignition.

quiz.q: State the two conditions that put combustion in the low-NOx, low-soot window.
quiz.a: No rich parcels (lean or well-mixed charge) and a peak temperature below about 2000 K, held there by dilution.

quiz.q: Why does a conventional diesel face a soot–NOx trade-off?
quiz.a: Its rich spray core makes soot and its near-stoichiometric flame sheet makes NOx. Cooling with EGR cuts NOx but lets soot survive; more air or heat burns soot but raises NOx.

quiz.q: Why does HCCI give high HC and CO at light load?
quiz.a: The charge is very lean and cool, so the coolest parts near the walls and in crevices never complete their reactions.

quiz.q: For E/R = 15 000 K, by what factor is the ignition delay shorter at 930 K than at 900 K?
An RCCI engine burns 21 mg of iso-octane and 9 mg of n-heptane per cycle. Find the global PRF.
Why does RCCI reach a wider load range than HCCI?
quiz.a: HCCI has no direct lever on ignition and burns its whole charge at once, so it rings at high load and misfires at low load. RCCI can change its fuel ratio and diesel timing every cycle; at high load a less reactive charge ignites later and burns more slowly through the reactivity gradient.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research now combines these ideas: partially premixed combustion with petrol-like fuels in diesel engines, gasoline compression ignition, and closed-loop control that reads cylinder pressure every cycle to hold the burn. Search next for “partially premixed combustion”, “gasoline compression ignition” and “cylinder-pressure-based combustion control”.

figure.caption: A sketch of the φ–T map of local gas states. Soot forms in the rich island, NOx in the hot band; a conventional diesel spray passes through both. HCCI and RCCI keep every parcel lean and below about 2000 K, so both stay low; PCCI moves the spray partway there.

spec.aria: Map with local temperature from 1000 to 3000 kelvin across and local equivalence ratio from 0 to 6 up. A shaded soot island sits at equivalence ratio above 2 between 1600 and 2600 kelvin; a NOx region fills temperatures above 2200 kelvin at lean mixtures. A dashed box at lean mixtures below 2000 kelvin is labelled HCCI and RCCI. A curved path for a conventional diesel spray crosses both regions.
